entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Zakkur, an Aramean king of Hamath and Luhuti, reigned in northern Syria around 785 BCE, a pivotal period marked by the waning influence of the Neo-Hittite states and the ascendance of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. His reign is primarily illuminated by the Stele of Zakkur, a basalt monument discovered in 1903, which provides a rare first-person account of a minor Syro-Hittite ruler facing a formidable coalition of rivals. This inscription offers invaluable insights into the complex geopolitical landscape of the early 8th century BCE Levant, detailing military conflicts, divine intervention, and the strategic alliances that shaped the region before full Assyrian domination.

The Stele of Zakkur recounts a major siege against Hamath led by Bar-Hadad III, king of Aram-Damascus, at the head of a coalition of sixteen kings, including those from Sam'al, Que, Gurgum, and other northern Syrian polities. Zakkur attributes his survival and victory to the intervention of the god Ba'al-shamayn, who answered his prayers and empowered him to withstand the siege and ultimately repel the invaders. This military success allowed Zakkur to maintain the independence of Hamath and Luhuti, at least temporarily, against a powerful alliance that sought to curb his growing influence, likely spurred by his expansion into the fertile plain of Luhuti.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Zakkur's successful defense of Hamath against a major coalition provided a crucial, rare first-person account of Iron Age Syro-Hittite political and military dynamics, influencing our understanding of regional power struggles before Assyrian hegemony. The Stele of Zakkur remains a cornerstone for studying Aramean language, religion, and inter-state relations.
